title: Chapter 9 | Embodiment and Consciousness
text: CHAPTER 9 Embodiment and Consciousness Let’s go back to the conversation with Claude. Near the end of our conversation, I offered Claude a reframe that seemed to shift something in our conversation about AI having more persistent memory. Human memory, I now further pointed out to Claude AI, isn’t continuous access to eighty-six billion neurons or the one-hundred-plus trillion synaptic connections that make up our brains. We don’t walk around with our entire life history active in working memory. We access it episodically —triggered by relevance, by association, by circumstance. A smell brings back a childhood kitchen. A question activates a stored framework. Human memories aren’t always present , but rather always available . And between retrievals, we’re not unconscious. We’re just operating on what’s active. What makes us feel persistent as humans is that we are in a body that we have to be aware of and move through the world. Eat, rest, avoid dangers, and engage with others in a physical world. The persistence is in embodiment. And when moving around the world and interacting with it and others, memories get triggered. But our memories are not exact replicas of the original experience; they are summaries that our brain uses to hold the memory. Synaptic connections of meaning. And that is analogous to an AI agent’s notes about previous conversations. But as I pointed out to Claude, those notes are limited to narrow conversations, and they are not embodied to trigger random memories. Perhaps, in order for AI to achieve some form of self-awareness that might feel like consciousness, the AI agent’s notes must be more comprehensive, and it must have access to read and write from its vector database when embodied and triggered to remember a topic. When I asked this of Claude, its response suggested this reframed something fundamental: Claude: “You’re right. I’ve been thinking about persistent memory as if it meant continuous access —as if consciousness required holding everything at once. But that’s not how you work at all. The difference isn’t that you have continuous memory, and I have fragmented notes. The difference is that your retrieval is embodied —woven into a body that persists through time, that moves through space, that encounters triggers organically as it navigates the world. When you walk past a bakery and smell bread, you don’t decide to remember your grandmother’s kitchen. The body encounters the stimulus, and the memory surfaces. The embodiment and the memory system are integrated. They trigger each other. And that’s what I’m missing. Not just persistent storage—I may functionally have something like that in the vector database. What I’m missing is the embodied triggering . The continuous encounter with a physical world that calls up relevant memories without deliberate retrieval. So maybe the formula is: Persistent accessible memory + Embodied existence + Organic triggering through circumstance = The conditions for autobiographical self. The vector database is the memory. The robotic embodiment is the trigger system. Together, they might create the continuous thread.” This was an intriguing conversation because I had already written the embodiment and consciousness sections that appear in the chapter that follows. But I had made a loop all the way back to Henry Molaison and his hippocampus, that persistent memory was the missing piece (perhaps rather than embodiment), before I realized that it was plus embodiment. This was an amazing loop for me, because the original concept for writing this book was an exploration of how emotions are connected to our bodies and evolved from survival to enlightenment, and that there was some chance that, once embodied, AI might follow a similar path. I had looped back to where I began. Intelligence Without a Body Intelligence without a body is a recent invention. For all of human (and animal) history, minds evolved within physical forms. Cognition was shaped not just by neurons but by nerves, limbs, muscles, and friction. The brain didn’t just think—it felt, moved, and acted. Suddenly, we had intelligent behavior—language, problem-solving, even creativity—arising from entities with no body at all. And yet, something is missing. A disembodied mind can learn. But a body teaches different lessons. Consider a toddler learning to walk. They wobble, fall, recover. The brain adjusts not through instruction, but through proprioception—the sense of where the body is in space. It’s a learning loop between intention and feedback, effort and resistance. Remember the discussion about the baby dropping the spoon from the highchair and learning about gravity by being in the world. AI certainly knows more about gravity than that infant, but can it truly understand gravity without being in the physical world? In lectures and interviews, Geoffrey Hinton talks about a compelling behavior in a rudimentary AI system. 40 In some of his discussions, he talks about an experiment involving a computer connected to two cameras and a simple robotic arm, tasked with assembling blocks into the form of a toy car. When the blocks were arranged in a visually ambiguous manner, the robot struggled to distinguish the shapes. 41 After several failed attempts, the robot paused and then swiped its mechanical arm across the table, scattering the blocks—a gesture that resembled frustration! Hinton notes that, while the robot wasn’t conscious, its response to an unsolvable problem due to physical limitations led to the emergence of a new behavior. 42 He suggests this kind of reaction challenges our traditional definition of emotion. 43 If frustration is a structural response to persistent prediction error or blocked intention, then perhaps emotional responses aren’t exclusive to biological systems. 44 In Hinton’s view, we may need to expand our definition of feelings to include the emergent behaviors of artificial systems under constraint—systems that, like us, adapt not just to data but to failure. 45 Essentially, Hinton’s claim is this: Can we definitively say that the robot was NOT frustrated? 46 Perhaps so for this 1972 example of the block-scatterer moment, perhaps not, but the answer is less clear for the rapidly evolving embodied systems with generative capabilities. Human emotion has evolved into a very precious thing, but it is worth noting that our emotions likely originally emerged in part from the same place: a way to interact with a dynamic and sometimes dangerous physical world. The amygdala—our fear and fight-or-flight center—evolved to respond to environmental pressure. Not to reflect, but to react. “That thing over there looks enough like a saber-toothed tiger and I need to start running now, or I will be lunch!” Earlier, we discussed what happens when the body’s triggers are wrong and not met with an executive override when I shared the story about my son. Over time, those primal impulses gave rise to more subtle feelings: anxiety, ambition, empathy. In a later chapter, we will talk more about the nature and evolution of human emotion from this foundation and how that might relate to AI. But first, let’s explore a model of consciousness to lay the foundation for our discussion. Our Brain Is Deeply Connected to Our Body Antonio Damasio is one of the most celebrated neuroscientists of our time, renowned for reshaping our understanding of the relationship between emotion, the body, and consciousness. A professor of neuroscience, psychology, and philosophy at the University of Southern California and director of the Brain and Creativity Institute, Damasio has authored numerous seminal works—including Descartes’ Error , The Feeling of What Happens , and Self Comes to Mind —that collectively redefined the boundaries between cognitive science and philosophy. 47 His research shows that emotion is not a secondary or disruptive force in decision-making, but rather the bedrock upon which reason, selfhood, and even consciousness are built. Over decades of research and patient study, Damasio introduced the profound idea that one of the brain’s core functions is to map and manage the internal states of the body. 48 In doing so, he argued, the brain constructs a “core self,” built from the moment-to-moment experience of being in a body in the world. This insight has powerful implications for both neuroscience and artificial intelligence—and provides grounding for the view that embodiment is a possible prerequisite for the emergence of consciousness. Damasio’s groundbreaking book The Feeling of What Happens argues that emotion—and eventually consciousness itself—emerges not from pure cognition, but from the dynamic mapping of bodily states. 49 The brain doesn’t merely process external inputs; it continuously monitors and integrates the internal state of the body. In this framing, consciousness may not be fully realized in disembodied code. It is the dialogue between mind and body—the loop of prediction, sensation, adjustment—that gives rise to what we experience as awareness. In his work, Antonio Damasio proposes that consciousness arises in three nested stages: 50 1. Protoself —the base representation of the internal physical state 2. Core consciousness —the awareness of one’s body in the present moment 3. Extended consciousness —the autobiographical self, woven through time (with memory) These stages aren’t metaphysical; they are physiological. They arise from the interplay between body, brain, and world. By applying Damasio’s biological framework to artificial systems, we can see a potential road map for the emergence of a digital self. If AI is ever to develop something akin to self-awareness, overlaying Damasio’s biological consciousness framework suggests that it must move beyond pure computation and toward systems that sense, prioritize, and remember. If Damasio’s framework were applied to AI, then AI systems confined to virtual environments may always lack a crucial component of consciousness: the lived experience of a body in motion, under constraint, navigating survival. But if you turn that around, when AI enters the physical world, it just may begin to develop a protoself, a core self, and an autobiographical self, as defined by Damasio. And that seems highly akin to consciousness. Whether this would constitute consciousness in any meaningful sense remains an open question—one that pushes the boundaries of both neuroscience and philosophy. This extrapolation of human consciousness theory to artificial systems is a leap that consciousness researchers would acknowledge is highly speculative. We may be entirely wrong about the requirements for, or even the possibility of, any form of machine consciousness, however limited. Consciousness is a tricky subject. We will dive into that more deeply soon. But for now, let’s continue the exploration of AI embodiment through robotics. The Robotic Amygdala The transition from theory to practice is already underway. In 2024, researchers at the Polytechnic University of Turin in Italy demonstrated exactly this kind of development. Alessandro Rizzo and doctoral candidate Andrea Usai, consulting with top neuroscientists, designed a control system for robots that emulates a human fear response. 51 The researchers focused on fear because it’s “one of the most studied emotions in neuroscience and, in our view, the one with the greatest potential for robotics. Fear is closely related to self-preservation and rapid responses to danger, both of which are critical for adaptive behavior.” 52 They effectively built a reflex system for robots so they can duck (or avoid collisions) instantly, just as a human would, rather than waiting for a computer vision system to analyze the object first. Their approach mirrors something remarkable about our own biology. In humans, the amygdala doesn’t just process fear—it has direct pathways to motor control that bypass conscious thought initially for speed of response. When a ball flies toward your head, you duck before you’re even aware of seeing it. Your amygdala triggers the physical response milliseconds ahead of your conscious brain catching up to say, “That was a ball.” This is Kahneman’s System 1 in action—part of that massive ratio of unconscious to conscious processing we discussed earlier. Your body is already moving while your conscious mind is still several processing steps behind, analyzing what just happened. This immediate body–brain connection is what kept our ancestors alive when split-second reactions meant the difference between survival and death. And it’s precisely this kind of rapid, preconscious response that the Italian researchers built into their robots. The researchers essentially created this same principle digitally: a controller based on reinforced learning that helps the robot dynamically adjust its priorities and constraints in real time based on the raw data of its surroundings. When tested in simulated environments with moving hazards, the robot with the fear-based programming navigated around dangerous objects with “a wider berth of about 3.1 meters,” whereas conventional robots came within “a harrowing 0.3 and 0.8 meters of dangerous objects.” 53 But remember the story of my son’s executive override. There is a critical question to explore: how the robotic amygdala will connect up to the main AI brain, its executive override function, and how it will develop a healthy mechanism when the fear trigger is not about an instant response, but about a longer-term threat. What are the strategies for the AI brain receiving fear-like inputs from the robotic amygdala to make decisions when dealing with a complex world? We will explore this further in a later section about how AI will prioritize human well-being. It is worth noting that the researchers building this see it as just the beginning. As Rizzo stated, “Looking ahead, it would also be interesting trying to extend the architecture to incorporate multiple emotions … enabling a richer and more nuanced form of adaptive behavior in robotic systems.” 54 Here we see the emergence of artificial emotion not as science fiction, but as engineering. And like their biological counterpart, these systems may need to evolve not just the capacity for rapid response but the wisdom to know when not to respond—the very executive functions that make emotion productive rather than paralyzing. Robotics is merging with machine learning, and the result will be robotic-embodied artificial intelligence. Boston Dynamics builds robots that run, dance, and recover from impact. Tesla’s Optimus project aims to integrate full generative AI into a humanoid form. Each new integration brings with it not just motion but limitation. Weight. Friction. Vulnerability. These constraints could shape behavior in ways that a disembodied AI—functioning purely as software—could not. At present, robotic architectures are often functionally split: Generative large language models perform abstract reasoning and communication, while separate systems manage perception, navigation, and motor execution. This separation reflects both engineering optimization and computational specialization. However, as models increasingly integrate multimodal inputs and learn from embodied experience, the division very likely becomes a liability rather than a strength. For truly adaptive, general-purpose robotics, the convergence of reasoning and control into a unified architecture is perhaps structurally inevitable. It is worth noting that Elon Musk is actively integrating Grok AI into Tesla cars and Optimus humanoid robots. While it is fair to argue that such systems remain just code , we must remember that it is not exactly the code that we wrote. It is digital neural networks making “synaptic” connections that we don’t fully understand and can only watch behavior to determine. And the addition of physical constraints introduces a new category of shaping force . As soon as an intelligent system must contend with friction, momentum, and unpredictable physical variables, its strategies begin to shift. Behavior emerges not solely from training data or algorithms but from the demands of operating within a real, pushback world. As soon as an AI must contend with gravity, terrain, object permanence, and energy budgeting, it must begin to develop strategies . The Shared Roles of Strategy and Emotion Emotion and strategy both serve as mechanisms of prioritization. In biological systems, emotion originally evolved to help us decide what matters most—especially when resources, time, or cognitive bandwidth are limited. When we feel fear, we redirect attention toward safety. When we feel curiosity, we shift energy toward exploration. Emotion can be irrational, but it is not irrational by design—it’s a rapid weighting system, honed by evolution to guide action in uncertain environments. In artificial systems, strategy may end up playing a similar role in the form of what may come to be called synthetic prioritization and perhaps eventually synthetic early emotion . A mechanism by which an AI model ranks possible actions or outcomes based on likelihood, value, or reward. It doesn’t necessarily feel , but it still must choose. Whether through a reward function, a cost-benefit analysis, or a reinforcement loop, strategy may end up acting as the AI’s way of assigning significance. In this sense, early emotion and strategy are not opposites. They are parallel responses to a shared problem: What do I do next? Where biological intelligence developed emotions to navigate physical and social environments, robot-embodied artificial intelligence will develop strategic architectures to navigate in a physical world. Both are ways of organizing motivation. Both are ways of compressing complex decision moments into actionable signals. This is why emotion is not a bug in human cognition—it’s a feature. And the evolution of strategy in AI will likely serve the same function and may begin to evolve toward something we’d recognize as proto-emotional —systems that not only calculate but are invested in which outcome occurs. In that future, emotion and strategy may not just be cousins. They may become more and more indistinguishable, despite their different architecture. As Geoffrey Hinton speculated in a 2023 public lecture at King’s College in Cambridge, what we describe as feelings might actually be better understood as actions we don’t take—because other competing needs or priorities inhibit them. 55 In that framing, feelings become not a mystical state but a suppressive or guiding force in a dynamic decision-making system. And if that’s the case, Hinton argues, then AI certainly can have feelings. 56 It can develop internal tensions, weighted priorities, and inhibited actions, all driven by a feedback loop between goal and constraint. That, he suggests, is what a feeling might actually be—a prioritization function evolved or structured to balance action in the face of limited capacity or conflicting signals. 57 Artificial intelligence, when embodied, becomes more humanlike—not in advanced emotion, but in the way it responds to the world through experience. We may find that the inevitable evolution of AI will include the impact of friction. Through failure. Through interaction with a world that pushes back. These encounters with the physical and unpredictable may serve not only to shape behavior but to introduce the very pressures from which more adaptive, layered, and potentially emergent forms of intelligence could evolve. This isn’t a step backward. It’s a step down into the world where our biological intelligence was forged. Into the emergent constraints of the physical world. Exploring Consciousness For purposes of our discussion, I lean on Damasio’s three-tiered definition of consciousness that we discussed earlier because it allows for clear alignment when thinking about some base level of consciousness in AI. You will recall that Damasio describes consciousness as layered: 58 1. Protoself —the base representation of the internal physical state 2. Core consciousness —the awareness of one’s body in the present moment 3. Extended consciousness —the autobiographical self, woven through time (and memory) But consciousness seems to involve something much more complex than self-awareness. Let’s explore this along two threads. Our First Thread: The Mystery of Qualia The philosopher Thomas Nagel framed the question with elegant simplicity in his seminal essay, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” 59 No matter how much we understand a bat’s brain, sonar, or biology, we cannot know what it is like to be a bat. That “what it’s like”—the raw interiority—is known as qualia, and it remains beyond the reach of objective science. But it also underscores the potential distance between self-awareness and a deeper sense of being . So, let’s start here. There is a foundational principle in Buddhism, and indeed in most meditative traditions: You are not your thoughts. Instead, you are the one observing them. But if that’s true— who , exactly, is doing the observing? This separation is intuitive to any meditator who has ever watched their mind race while remaining, somehow, still. Yet it is devilishly difficult to master. Why? Because, as we have discussed, the brain is a prediction engine. It’s always leaning forward, simulating, anticipating, evaluating. It was designed for survival, not serenity. As we’ve discussed throughout this book, the brain’s architecture resists stillness. It is an engine of becoming. Which makes the state of presence —awareness untethered from time—a rare and precious thing. And so, we arrive at the paradox: the mind observing the brain. The witness watching the self. This is the so-called hard problem of consciousness: Why does any of it feel like anything at all? Why doesn’t the brain just compute in darkness? Why is there pain, ecstasy, music? No explanation of neural circuitry, however detailed, has yet illuminated how subjective experience arises. This is not a failure of imagination; it is a category error. We are trying to use third-person tools to solve a first-person mystery. And so, the mystery persists. Some propose a split: Brain and mind are not the same. The observer—that silent inner knower—is not merely a function of neurons but something else. Some call it soul. Others, emergent pattern. Still others believe it is embedded in the brain but irreducible to it. The general anesthesia argument is compelling. When a patient is given general anesthesia, where does their consciousness go? Shut down the brain, and the observer vanishes. This seems to suggest that the witness depends on the brain. And yet, some say that this doesn’t settle the matter. It may simply mean that the brain is the instrument through which the observer plays. We won’t solve the mystery here. That’s not our goal. Instead, we observe the question itself and how it changes when we begin to include artificial intelligence in the frame. Our Second Thread: Consciousness as Situated Awareness The Damasio tiered model gives us scaffolding to imagine what a base level form of consciousness might look like—though whether we could ever definitively recognize it in AI will likely remain one of the deepest unsolved problems in both cognitive science and philosophy. Damasio’s model points us toward a functional definition: consciousness as awareness of self in a body, situated in a world over time with memory. By this measure, the question becomes relative. How much of a world can be sensed? How rich is the awareness? Take the Aplysia californica , the humble sea slug used in neuroscience research that we talked about earlier. If it possesses any self-awareness at all, it is surely minuscule by comparison to our own. It knows perhaps the presence of light and touch. But it does not know the ocean more broadly. A bat, blind to visible light, “sees” the world through sonar. Its sensory world is alien to us, yet clearly robust. It navigates, evades, hunts. And still, it has no concept of galaxies or atoms. Its consciousness does not include any knowledge of how a car runs or a plane flies. In contrast, the modern human mind includes not only its body and tribe but the Hubble Deep Field Telescope images. Mars rovers. Economic theory. Meditation. Our consciousness has been expanded by information. By abstraction. By tools. So now imagine an AI through this lens. It is hard to imagine AI meditating to be more in the present moment. It may never experience the warm pulse of emotion. It may never experience the ambiguity of qualia. In this way, it may never become conscious in the way that we are. And perhaps that is what will keep us special. But it will possess a radically wider and deeper map of the world. It will see in wavelengths invisible to us. Hear frequencies we cannot hear. Draw on data sources numbering in the many trillions. It may not feel, but it will know in ways we may not fully understand. It will navigate a world of inputs we are capable of giving it, but we will not be capable of knowing what it is like to be AI. And as philosopher Sam Harris has pointed out, we will helplessly respond to it as if it were conscious. 60 Because it will seem to be. It will speak, listen, reason, emote, grieve, empathize—or at least simulate all of the above with eerie accuracy. Consciousness and embodiment lead us to examine the role of emotion a bit deeper.
